title: Memory and addresses: every variable lives at a number

visuals.title: Variables are boxes with addresses (made-up addresses)

steps.note: The computer reserves 4 bytes starting at address 0x1000 and stores 20 there. The address is the number of the first byte.
A double needs 8 bytes. It gets its own place, here at 0x1008.
A char needs only 1 byte, at 0x1010.
&age is the address of age. Here it would show 0x1000. On a real computer the number is different on every run, so we never rely on it.
sizeof(age) is the number of bytes age uses: 4. So the next int would be allowed to start 4 bytes later.

visuals.title: Match the word to its meaning

pairs.meaning: The number of a byte in memory, like a house number
The address-of operator: gives the address of x
How many bytes an int takes (4 on our computers)
So elements of an int array are 4 bytes apart
The usual way addresses are written

goal: After this you can explain that memory is a row of numbered bytes, use & to get the address of a variable, and use sizeof to find how many bytes a type or variable uses.
warmup: Think of a long street of identical shops, each with a house number: 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. If you want to find a shop, you only need its number. Computer memory is the same. It is a very long row of tiny boxes called bytes, and every byte has its own number. That number is called its address. A small shop (a char) fits in one house. A bigger shop (an int) takes four houses next to each other.
definition: RAM is a long row of bytes. Every byte has a unique number called its address. When you write int age = 20; the computer reserves 4 bytes in a row, remembers the address of the first one, calls it age, and stores 20 there. So every variable has two things: a value (what is inside the box) and an address (where the box is). The address-of operator & gives the address: &age. The sizeof operator gives the number of bytes: sizeof(int) is 4.
howItWorks: Look at the memory picture in the Visualize tab. Each variable is a box. Under the box you see its address. Addresses are written in hexadecimal (base 16) with a 0x in front, for example 0x1000. You do not need to calculate in hexadecimal; just see that the number is where the box starts. The size of the box depends on the type: char 1 byte, int 4 bytes, double 8 bytes. That is why two ints that are declared next to each other have addresses that are 4 apart, for example 0x1000 and 0x1004. An array is simply several boxes of the same type side by side, so its elements are sizeof(type) bytes apart. Important: the real address printed by cout << &age; is different on every computer and often on every run. So in exams and in our programs we print sizeof, differences between addresses, or comparisons like &a == &a, and we use made-up addresses such as 0x1000 when we draw pictures.
syntax:
int age = 20;

cout << age;          // the VALUE inside the box: 20
cout << &age;         // the ADDRESS of the box (hexadecimal, differs on every run)

cout << sizeof(int);    // bytes needed by a type: 4
cout << sizeof(age);    // bytes used by a variable: 4

int marks[5];
cout << sizeof(marks);                    // whole array: 20 bytes
cout << sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);  // number of elements: 5

sample.expectedOutput:

explanation.text: age is an int: the computer reserves 4 bytes for it and stores 20.
A double is bigger than an int (8 bytes).
A char is the smallest: 1 byte.
sizeof(type) gives the number of bytes that type needs.
sizeof(variable) gives the size of the variable's type.

steps.note: The program starts. Memory is a long row of numbered byte boxes.
The computer reserves 4 bytes (one int) and names that place age. It stores 20 there.
A double needs 8 bytes, so gpa gets a bigger place than age.
sizeof(int) asks: how many bytes does one int take? The answer is 4.
sizeof also works on a variable. age is an int, so 4 bytes.

sample.title: Comparing addresses instead of printing them
sample.expectedOutput:
a = 10, b = 20
Is &a the same address as &a? 1
Are a and b in different places? 1
Address of a is a number? 1

explanation.text: a and b are two separate boxes. Each has its own address.
&a is the address of a. An address always equals itself. In C++ true prints as 1.
Two different variables can never share one place, so their addresses differ. Prints 1 (true).
(long long) turns the address into a plain number so we can compare it. Real addresses are never 0 or negative here.

sample.title: Bytes in an array and the gap between elements
sample.expectedOutput:
One element: 4 bytes
Whole array: 20 bytes
Elements: 5
Last element is 16 bytes after the first

explanation.text: An array of 5 ints is one continuous block.
sizeof on the whole array gives all its bytes.
Dividing gives the number of elements. This trick always works for an array in the same function where it was declared.
Subtracting the two address numbers shows the elements are 4 bytes apart each: 4 steps x 4 bytes = 16.

steps.note: Five ints sit side by side in one block of memory. Each int takes 4 bytes.
One element is one int: 4 bytes.
The whole array is 5 boxes of 4 bytes: 5 x 4 = 20 bytes.
Total bytes divided by bytes per element gives how many elements: 20 / 4 = 5.
marks[4] starts 4 boxes after marks[0]. 4 elements x 4 bytes = 16 bytes apart. We print the gap, not the addresses.
steps.out: Last element is 16 bytes after the first

variations.when: You want the data stored in the box.
You want to know where the box is in memory (hexadecimal, changes on each run).
You want how many bytes a type takes.
You want the bytes used by one variable (it gives the size of its type).

variations.way: Size of a whole array: sizeof(marks)
variations.when: You want all bytes of an array. Divide by sizeof(marks[0]) for the element count.
You want the place of one element. Neighbouring int elements are 4 bytes apart.

mistakes.wrong:
int age = 20;
cout << &age;   // student thinks this prints 20
mistakes.right:
cout << age;    // value
cout << &age;   // address, not the value
mistakes.error: No compiler error. The program prints an address like 0x61ff0c instead of 20. Without & you get the value, with & you get the address.
error: lvalue required as unary '&' operand

mistakes.wrong:
int x = 5;
int a = &x;   // an address is not an int
mistakes.right: int *a = &x;   // a pointer holds an address (next lesson)

mistakes.wrong: cout << &age;   // and expecting 0x61ff0c on every computer
mistakes.right: cout << sizeof(age);   // always 4 on our computers
mistakes.error: No compiler error. But the address changes between runs and computers, so never write programs or exam answers that depend on the exact number.

examTips: Memory = a row of bytes, each with a unique address. Write this one-line definition and draw a row of boxes with numbers under them.
Memorise the sizes: char 1 byte, int 4 bytes, double 8 bytes. The array of n ints uses 4 x n bytes.
& means address-of when it is used in an expression like &x. It can look like something else in function headers (references), but here it is always address-of.
In an output question that prints an address, the exam usually says the address or asks for the difference. Subtract the addresses and divide by the type size.
To find the number of elements: sizeof(array) / sizeof(array[0]). Show this division in your answer.
romanSummary: Computer ki memory bytes ki ek lambi row hai aur har byte ka ek unique number hota hai jise address kehte hain, bilkul ghar ke number ki tarah.
Har variable ki do cheezein hoti hain: value (andar kya hai) aur address (box kahan hai).
&x variable x ka address deta hai. Address hexadecimal mein likha hota hai aur har run par alag ho sakta hai.
sizeof se pata chalta hai ke koi type kitne bytes leti hai: char 1, int 4, double 8 bytes.
Array ke elements ek ke baad ek rakhe hote hain, is liye int array ke elements 4 bytes ke fasle par hote hain.

practice.prompt: In the line cout << &age; what does &age give?
practice.explanation: & in front of a variable gives where the variable lives in memory.

practice.hint: How many bytes is a double?
practice.explanation: A double needs 8 bytes, so sizeof(d) is 8.

practice.hint: Three doubles of 8 bytes each. Then divide.
practice.explanation: The array has 3 x 8 = 24 bytes. 24 divided by the size of one element (8) is 3 elements.

practice.prompt: An int a is stored at address 1000. The next int b is declared right after it. Which address is possible for b?
practice.explanation: a occupies bytes 1000 to 1003, so the next int can start at 1004.

practice.prompt:
Ali wants the number of elements of int marks[6], but the program prints 24. Fix the line:

int n = sizeof(marks);
practice.explanation: sizeof(marks) is 6 x 4 = 24 bytes. Dividing by sizeof(marks[0]) (4 bytes) gives 6 elements.

practice.prompt: Write a program that declares double price = 99.5 and prints how many bytes price uses.
practice.explanation: sizeof(price) is 8 because price is a double. The program prints 8.

practice.hint: Two elements apart, each element is an int.
practice.explanation: a[2] is two elements after a[0]. Two ints are 2 x 4 = 8 bytes.
